title: The House Behind the Cedars
description: Published in 1900 and the classic American novel of racial passing: the story of a brother and sister who pass for white in South Carolina and of the catastrophe that follows.
plot_or_argument: Rena Rena Walden, who is three-quarters white, passes as white in the town of Clarence and is courted by the white lawyer George Tryon; when her identity is revealed he abandons her, and she dies of fever after a self-sacrificing attempt to save her friend, while her brother John renounces his white life.
historical_context: The 1900: the South Carolina of the 1890s, the one-drop rule and the racial law of the American South.
literary_significance: The House Behind the Cedars is the central American novel of passing and a key text in the literature of race: its treatment of the tragedy of racial classification made it the model for the twentieth-century American novel of passing from Larsen to Roth.

title: The Colonel's Dream
description: Published in 1905 and Chesnutt's most ambitious novel: the return of a southern colonel to rebuild his home town after the Civil War, and the defeat of his plan by the racial order.
plot_or_argument: Colonel French returns to North Carolina with northern capital and the intention of modernising the mills and educating the black workers; he is defeated by the old aristocracy, the convict labour system and the racial hatred of the town, and the novel ends with his departure and the death of a black child.
historical_context: The 1905: the New South programme, the convict lease system, and the failure of Reconstruction in the southern economy.
literary_significance: The Colonel's Dream is the finest American novel of the New South and one of the most radical works of American social criticism of its time: its analysis of the economic interests behind segregation makes it a key text in the literature of American race and capitalism.

title: Lyrics of Lowly Life
description: Published in 1896 with an introduction by William Dean Howells and the book that made Dunbar famous: the dialect poems of the old plantation and the standard English lyrics of love, grief and race.
plot_or_argument: The collection includes 'The Old Cabin', 'A Banjo Song', 'When Malindy Sings', 'Sympathy' ('I know what the caged bird feels'), 'We Wear the Mask', and the elegy 'Frederick Douglass'.
literary_form: Poetry collection (with an introduction by William Dean Howells)
historical_context: The 1896: the American plantation tradition, the Chicago World's Fair of 1893, and the black literary market of the 1890s.
literary_significance: Lyrics of Lowly Life is the founding book of African-American poetry and the volume through which Dunbar became the first black American poet of national reputation: 'We Wear the Mask' and 'Sympathy' are among the most important poems in American literature.

title: 'We Wear the Mask'
description: Written in 1895 and published in Majors and Minors and then in Lyrics of Lowly Life: the central American poem of the mask, in which the black speaker addresses a deceitful world.
plot_or_argument: The speaker describes the mask that 'grins and lies' and hides the cheeks and eyes of a people who smile while their torn hearts bleed, and asks Christ only that the world be not allowed to see beyond the mask.
literary_form: Lyric poem (in Majors and Minors, 1895; Lyrics of Lowly Life, 1896)
meter_and_prosody: Three five-line stanzas of iambic tetrameter and trimeter, rhymed aabba, with a refrain.
historical_context: The 1890s: the Jim Crow South, the politics of accommodation, and the double consciousness of the black American.
literary_significance: 'We Wear the Mask' is the central American poem about race and concealment and one of the most quoted poems in English: its image of the mask has become the key term of African-American literary criticism, and it is the founding text of the literature of double consciousness.

title: The Sport of the Gods
description: Published in 1902 and Dunbar's finest novel: the destruction of a respectable black family by a false accusation, and their migration to New York.
plot_or_argument: Berry Hamilton, a faithful servant, is imprisoned for a theft committed by his employer's brother; his wife and children move to New York, where his daughter falls into the theatre and prostitution and his son into gambling, and the family is destroyed before the truth is discovered.
principal_characters: Berry Hamilton; Fannie Hamilton; Joe Hamilton; Kitty Hamilton; Maurice Oakley; Francis Oakley; Sadness
historical_context: The 1902: the black migration to northern cities, the New York of the Tenderloin, and the American naturalist novel.
literary_significance: The Sport of the Gods is the first major African-American novel of urban naturalism and one of the founding texts of the literature of the Great Migration: its picture of the city's destruction of a black family is unmatched in its period.

title: Majors and Minors
description: Published in 1895 and the volume that brought Dunbar to Howells's attention: the first collection to mix the dialect poems ('majors') with the standard English lyrics ('minors').
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'We Wear the Mask', 'Sympathy', 'The Path', 'A Summer's Night' and the dialect pieces that had made Dunbar popular in the Midwest, and its division between the two registers is the central fact of his career.
historical_context: The 1895: the black literary market, the Chicago of the World's Fair, and the American debate on dialect poetry.
literary_significance: Majors and Minors is the book that established Dunbar and the clearest statement of the double register of African-American poetry at the end of the nineteenth century; it is a central document in the history of black literary representation.

title: The Complete Poems of Paul Laurence Dunbar
description: Published in 1913 after his death and the standard collection of Dunbar's verse: the dialect poems, the standard English lyrics and the late poems of love and death.
plot_or_argument: The volume gathers the four major collections and the uncollected poems, and shows the full range of Dunbar's work — the plantation dialect that made him famous, the lyrics of 'The Debt', 'Slow through the Dark' and 'The Haunted Oak', and the poems of his last illness.
historical_context: The 1913: the posthumous reputation of Dunbar, the Harlem Renaissance to come, and the American canonisation of black poetry.
literary_significance: The Complete Poems is the standard text of the first African-American poet of national reputation and shows the full achievement behind the dialect reputation; it is essential to the history of American poetry and of black literature.

title: Little Women
description: Published in two parts in 1868 and 1869 and the most beloved American family novel: the lives of the four March sisters from adolescence to marriage.
plot_or_argument: Meg, Jo, Beth and Amy March grow up in genteel poverty in a New England town while their father is away at war; the novel follows their courtships, Jo's writing, Beth's illness and death, and their marriages, and ends with the family gathered at Marmee's birthday.
principal_characters: Meg March; Jo March; Beth March; Amy March; Marmee; Laurie Laurence; Mr Brooke; Professor Bhaer; Aunt March; Hannah
historical_context: The 1860s: the American Civil War, the New England village, and the market for girls' fiction after the war.
literary_significance: Little Women is the central American family novel and the most widely read girls' book in the world: its portrait of four sisters, its treatment of work and ambition, and its frankness about money and death made it the model for the American novel of growing up.

title: Hospital Sketches
description: Published in 1863 and based on Alcott's service as a nurse at the Union Hotel Hospital in Georgetown: the first great American book of the Civil War from a woman's point of view.
plot_or_argument: Tribulation Periwinkle, the narrator, travels to Washington, takes up her duties among the wounded, and records the deaths, the jokes and the ordinariness of the hospital, ending with her own illness and return home.
literary_form: Collection of letters (first published in the Commonwealth, 1863)
historical_context: The 1862-63: the Civil War, the Sanitary Commission, and the new profession of the woman nurse.
literary_significance: Hospital Sketches is the founding American narrative of the Civil War hospital and one of the first American books to treat nursing as a profession; its unsentimental record of death and its comic voice made it a model for the American literature of war and medicine.

title: Work: A Story of Experience
description: Published in 1873 and Alcott's most directly feminist novel: the story of a New England girl who must earn her own living and tries a series of occupations.
plot_or_argument: Christie Devon works as a servant, an actress, a seamstress, a governess and a companion, marries the reformer David Sterling, is widowed, and finally finds her vocation as a nurse and a woman of independent judgment.
historical_context: The 1870s: the new women's occupations, the American labour question, and the debate on women's work.
literary_significance: Work is the founding American novel of women's employment and one of the most important feminist novels of the nineteenth century: its survey of the occupations open to women and its insistence on economic independence made it a key text of the American women's movement.

title: Behind a Mask; or, A Woman's Power
description: Published anonymously in 1866 as by A. M. Barnard and the most subversive of Alcott's thrillers: the story of a governess who is not what she seems.
plot_or_argument: Jean Muir, a thirty-year-old actress, passes herself off as a nineteen-year-old governess in an aristocratic English family and systematically ensnares the heir, Sir Edward Coventry, exposing the vanity and cruelty of the household before she is unmasked and marries him anyway.
literary_form: Novella (published anonymously as A. M. Barnard)
historical_context: The 1860s: the sensation vogue, the governess question, and the American market for anonymous thrillers.
literary_significance: Behind a Mask is one of the boldest American stories of the 1860s and the key text in the recovery of Alcott's sensation fiction: its femme fatale heroine and its attack on the English aristocracy have made it central to the feminist reading of Alcott.

title: Little Men
description: Published in 1871 and the sequel to Little Women: the school for boys that Jo and Professor Bhaer establish at Plumfield.
plot_or_argument: Nat Blake, an orphaned musician, arrives at Plumfield and is followed by the street boy Dan; the novel follows the boys' education under Jo and Fritz, through their pranks, illnesses and moral crises, to the beginnings of their adult lives.
historical_context: The 1870s: the American common school, the Froebelian kindergarten movement, and the progressive education of the period.
literary_significance: Little Men is the classic American novel of progressive education and one of the founding texts of the American school story; its picture of Jo as a teacher and of the Plumfield experiment makes it a key document in the history of American education.

title: 'Life in the Iron-Mills'
description: Published in the Atlantic Monthly in April 1861, the month the Civil War began, and the founding text of American literary realism: a night in the life of an iron mill town.
plot_or_argument: Hugh Wolfe, a Welsh puddler, sculpts a figure of a woman out of the mill's waste korl and is accused of theft by his employer's son; his cousin Deborah takes the blame, and Hugh dies in prison, while the mill owner's daughter looks at the sculpture and understands nothing.
principal_characters: Hugh Wolfe; Deborah Wolfe; Janey; Kirby; Doctor May; Mitchell
historical_context: The 1850s-60s: the iron mills of Wheeling, the immigrant Welsh and Irish workers, and the American industrial revolution before the war.
literary_significance: 'Life in the Iron-Mills' is the first great American work of industrial fiction and the founding text of American realism: it preceded Howells, Garland and Dreiser by a generation, and its portrait of the worker's hunger for beauty is one of the permanent scenes of American literature.

title: Margret Howth: A Story of To-Day
description: Published in 1862 and the first American novel of the industrial working woman: the story of a mill town and of the woman who keeps her family alive by her labour.
plot_or_argument: Margret Howth works as a bookkeeper in a mill and cares for her blind father; she is loved by the mill owner Knowles and by her cousin Lois, and the novel moves between the town's poor and the mill's owners, ending with Margret's marriage and her commitment to the poor.
historical_context: The 1861-62: the American mill town, the first generation of women clerks, and the outbreak of the Civil War.
literary_significance: Margret Howth is the first American novel with a working woman as its heroine and one of the founding texts of the American literature of labour: its treatment of the economics of the single woman's life is unmatched in its period.

title: Waiting for the Verdict
description: Published in 1868 and Davis's novel of the Civil War and its racial aftermath: the story of a black surgeon and the family that passes for white.
plot_or_argument: Dr Brodie, a black surgeon serving with the Union army, and the white family of the Rossiters are bound by a secret of mixed ancestry; the novel follows the war, the nursing, the battle of Gettysburg and the reconstruction of the family, and ends with the verdict of the title still awaited.
historical_context: The 1863-68: the Civil War, the hospital and the field, emancipation, and the American debate on racial equality.
literary_significance: Waiting for the Verdict is one of the first American novels to treat a black professional as its hero and the first substantial American novel of the Civil War from a woman's perspective; it is a key text in the literature of race and Reconstruction.

title: Dallas Galbraith
description: Published in 1868 and the most ambitious American industrial novel before the age of naturalism: a story of the Pennsylvania iron country during the Civil War boom.
plot_or_argument: Dallas Galbraith, the son of an ironmaster, returns from Europe to find his family's mill in crisis; the novel follows the fortunes of the workers, the speculations of the owners and the marriage of Dallas to a woman who has her own ideas about money and work.
historical_context: The 1860s: the Pennsylvania iron and coal country, the Civil War demand for iron, and the beginning of the American labour movement.
literary_significance: Dallas Galbraith is the broadest American industrial novel of the 1860s and a significant predecessor of the naturalist novel of business; its analysis of the relation between capital, labour and the state makes it a key text in the literature of American industrialisation.

title: The Gates Ajar
description: Published in 1868 and the most popular American novel of consolation ever written: the diary of a young woman whose brother has been killed in the Civil War, and the vision of heaven that consoles her.
plot_or_argument: Mary Cabot is left desolate by the death of her brother Roy at Antietam; her aunt Winifred arrives and describes a heaven that is a continuation of earthly life, with houses, families, work and the reunion of the beloved, and Mary moves from grief to a faith that answers the orthodox teaching of her minister.
historical_context: The 1865-68: the American Civil War dead and the mourning of the nation, the New England ministry, and the spiritualist movement.
literary_significance: The Gates Ajar is the central American novel of mourning and the founding text of the consolatory literature of the post-war decade: it sold in the hundreds of thousands, was translated into many languages, and gave Victorian Americans a domestic heaven that answered the slaughter of the war.

title: The Story of Avis
description: Published in 1877 and the first great American novel of the woman artist: the story of a painter whose marriage destroys her vocation.
plot_or_argument: Avis Dobell, a gifted painter, marries the physician Philip Ostrander, and the novel follows the slow extinction of her art under the demands of marriage, motherhood and the care of a husband who does not understand her, until her death leaves her work unfinished.
principal_characters: Avis Dobell; Philip Ostrander; Professor Dobell; Sara Austyn; Coy; her children
historical_context: The 1870s: the American art world, the first generation of women artists and art students, and the debate on women's education.
literary_significance: The Story of Avis is the founding American novel of the conflict between marriage and artistic vocation and one of the most important feminist novels of the century: its portrait of the slow death of a woman's talent is unmatched in American fiction before Kate Chopin.

title: Doctor Zay
description: Published in 1882 and one of the first American novels with a woman physician as its heroine: the story of a doctor and her patient, and of the man who must learn to accept her profession.
plot_or_argument: Yale, a wealthy young man injured in an accident, is treated by Dr Zay, a woman physician of independent means and professional authority; he falls in love with her and must come to terms with a wife who will not give up her practice.
historical_context: The 1880s: the first generation of American women doctors, the women's medical colleges, and the debate on women's professional work.
literary_significance: Doctor Zay is the founding American novel of the woman doctor and a key text in the history of American women's professionalisation: its treatment of the marriage of equals makes it one of the most advanced feminist novels of the 1880s.

title: The Silent Partner
description: Published in 1871 and Phelps's industrial novel: the story of a New England mill owner's daughter who inherits the mill and the responsibility for its workers.
plot_or_argument: Perley Kelso, a Boston merchant's daughter, becomes part owner of a mill at the death of her father and takes an interest in the workers; the novel follows the mill girl Sip and the overseer Fly, and ends with Perley's decision to live as a single woman dedicated to the welfare of her workers.
historical_context: The 1870s: the New England textile mills, the first woman's trade unions, and the American debate on industrial paternalism.
literary_significance: The Silent Partner is one of the most important American novels of industrial labour between Davis and the naturalists and a founding text of the American novel of the woman reformer; its treatment of class, philanthropy and the single woman is unmatched in its period.

title: Poems on Miscellaneous Subjects
description: Published in 1854 with a preface by William Lloyd Garrison and the first book by an African-American woman poet: poems of slavery, freedom and Christian duty, written for the antislavery platform.
plot_or_argument: The volume contains 'The Slave Mother', 'Eliza Harris', 'The Slave Auction', 'Bury Me in a Free Land', 'A Mother's Heroism' and 'The Prodigal's Return', and its subjects are the sale of families, the fugitive's flight and the duty of the free North.
literary_form: Poetry collection (with a preface by William Lloyd Garrison)
historical_context: The 1854: the Fugitive Slave Law, the antislavery lecture circuit, and the free black community of the northern states.
literary_significance: Poems on Miscellaneous Subjects is the founding book of African-American women's poetry: 'Bury Me in a Free Land' is one of the great American abolitionist poems, and Harper's recitation of these verses made her one of the most important black voices of the 1850s.

title: Iola Leroy; or, Shadows Uplifted
description: Published in 1892 and the first novel by an African-American woman: the story of a beautiful mixed-race woman who is sold into slavery and of her life after emancipation.
plot_or_argument: Iola Leroy, raised as white and educated in the North, is kidnapped and sold as a slave when her father's death reveals her mother's ancestry; she is rescued during the war, works as a nurse, searches for her scattered family, and dedicates her life to the education and uplift of her people.
historical_context: The 1892: the post-Reconstruction South, the black women's club movement, and the debate on passing and racial loyalty.
literary_significance: Iola Leroy is the first novel by an African-American woman and the founding text of African-American women's fiction: its treatment of passing, its picture of black life in slavery and freedom, and its argument for racial loyalty make it a central document of American literature.

title: Moses: A Story of the Nile
description: Published in 1869 and Harper's most ambitious poem: a blank-verse life of Moses, written as an allegory of the emancipation of the slaves.
plot_or_argument: The poem follows Moses from his rescue in the bulrushes through his exile in Midian and the call at the burning bush to the exodus, the giving of the law and his death on Mount Nebo, and it reads the story of Israel as the story of the African-American people.
historical_context: The 1869: the Reconstruction of the South, the black church, and the use of the Exodus narrative in African-American culture.
literary_significance: Moses is one of the most ambitious American poems of the century and a founding text of the African-American literary use of the Bible: its identification of the black American with the enslaved Israel made the Exodus the central myth of black American religion and literature.

title: Sketches of Southern Life
description: Published in 1872 and Harper's most original contribution to American dialect poetry: the monologues of Aunt Chloe, a freedwoman of the South.
plot_or_argument: Aunt Chloe tells her own story in her own voice — the sale of her children, the war, emancipation, the founding of her school and her church, and her opinions of the Reconstruction politicians — in a series of poems that use dialect as a voice of authority rather than comedy.
historical_context: The 1872: the South during Reconstruction, the freedmen's schools, and the black church.
literary_significance: Sketches of Southern Life is the finest American dialect poetry of the Reconstruction era and the founding text of the black vernacular monologue: its use of Aunt Chloe's voice to record the black experience from inside reversed the minstrel convention and prepared the way for Dunbar and the twentieth-century black poets.

title: Our Nig; or, Sketches from the Life of a Free Black
description: Published in Boston in 1859 at the author's expense and the first novel by an African-American woman: a fictionalised autobiography of a mixed-race indentured servant in New Hampshire.
plot_or_argument: Alfrado, the daughter of a black man and a white woman, is abandoned at six and bound out to a New England family who treat her with systematic cruelty; she grows up in servitude, is prevented from attending school, has a child by a fugitive slave who abandons her, and writes her book to support herself and her son.
principal_characters: Frado (Alfrado); Mag Smith; Jim; Seth Shipley; Mrs Bellmont; Mary; Jack; Aunt Abby; James
literary_form: Novel (autobiographical; published at the author's expense in Boston)
historical_context: The 1840s-50s: the free black population of the North, the indentured child servant, and the abolitionist market of the 1850s.
literary_significance: Our Nig is the first American novel by an African-American woman and the first African-American novel to depict slavery's northern analogue in indentured servitude: its recovery in 1983 rewrote the history of African-American fiction and made Wilson a founding figure of the tradition.
